records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: A client retries a request after a timeout. Which HTTP methods can it safely repeat, and how would you design a POST endpoint that may be retried?
expected_topics: POST is not idempotent by default
idempotency key or natural key for POST

rubric.0: Cannot distinguish safe or idempotent methods, or claims every method is safe to retry.
rubric.1: Knows GET is safe but is vague about PUT/DELETE/POST behaviour on retry.
rubric.2: Correctly explains safe vs idempotent methods and why POST needs extra design to be retried.
rubric.3: Explains the semantics precisely and gives a concrete design (e.g. idempotency key, stored result) with trade-offs from real work.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: Walk me through how you choose HTTP status codes for an integration API, for example a duplicate create request versus invalid input.

rubric.0: Returns 200 for errors or cannot explain status code classes.
rubric.1: Distinguishes client and server errors but chooses codes inconsistently.
rubric.2: Chooses appropriate codes such as 409 for conflicts and explains how clients react.
rubric.3: Uses codes deliberately, ties them to client retry behaviour and a consistent machine-readable error format.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: Your integration starts receiving 429 responses from a partner API. What do you do in the client?

rubric.0: Suggests retrying immediately in a loop or ignoring the error.
rubric.1: Knows 429 means rate limited but has no concrete client strategy.
rubric.2: Honours Retry-After, adds backoff and limits concurrency.
rubric.3: Describes a measured strategy (budgeting, backoff with jitter, queueing, alerting) from a real incident.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: How do you return errors from an API so that client teams can handle them programmatically?

rubric.0: No structured error format; free-text or stack traces returned.
rubric.1: Has an error body but fields are ad hoc or leak internals.
rubric.2: Uses a consistent machine-readable error format with codes and helpful detail.
rubric.3: Designs a versioned error contract (e.g. RFC 9457 style), avoids leaking internals, and explains client handling.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: Explain the difference between a 401 and a 403 response, and give an integration example of each.

rubric.2: Correct distinction with realistic examples (expired token vs missing scope).
rubric.3: Correct distinction, examples, and how clients/monitoring should respond to each.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: How would one backend service authenticate to another service's API with OAuth 2.0, with no user involved?

rubric.1: Mentions tokens or API keys without explaining the flow.
rubric.2: Describes the client credentials grant, scopes and token expiry.
rubric.3: Describes the flow end to end including secret storage, token caching, rotation and failure handling.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: What precautions do you take when handling bearer tokens or API keys in an integration?

rubric.0: No awareness of token handling risks.
rubric.1: Mentions HTTPS but misses URL/log leakage or storage.
rubric.2: Covers TLS, keeping tokens out of URLs/logs and secure storage.
rubric.3: Explains the bearer threat model and concrete controls (rotation, scoping, secret manager, log redaction) used in practice.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: A partner asks to send their API key as a query parameter because it is easier. How do you respond?

rubric.1: Senses a risk but cannot explain it.
rubric.2: Explains URL logging risk and proposes header-based auth over HTTPS.
rubric.3: Explains the risk, proposes secure alternatives and how to roll the change out with the partner.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: How do you write database queries in integration code so that data from external systems cannot cause SQL injection?

rubric.0: Builds SQL by string concatenation or cannot explain injection.
rubric.1: Knows injection is a risk but the mitigation is vague (e.g. escaping only).
rubric.2: Uses parameterised queries and avoids concatenation.
rubric.3: Parameterised queries plus least privilege and validation, with an example from real code.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: An integration receives the same customer record several times. How would you write it to the database without creating duplicates?

rubric.0: Would insert every time or check-then-insert without considering races.
rubric.1: Mentions checking for existence first but ignores concurrency.
rubric.2: Uses a unique key with an atomic upsert.
rubric.3: Explains atomic upsert, race conditions and how this makes the consumer idempotent.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: What transaction isolation level does your database use by default, and when has isolation mattered in your work?
expected_topics: default isolation (e.g. Read Committed in PostgreSQL)

rubric.0: No understanding of transactions or isolation.
rubric.1: Knows transactions exist but not isolation levels or anomalies.
rubric.2: Names the default level and explains the anomalies it allows or prevents.
rubric.3: Gives a real case where isolation affected correctness and how it was resolved.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: Describe a SQL query you wrote to reconcile data between two systems. How did you check the result was correct?

rubric.1: Describes a query at a high level without verification.
rubric.2: Describes the query logic and a reasonable verification approach.
rubric.3: Specific query, edge cases (nulls, duplicates), verification and the outcome achieved.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: Your queue consumer can receive the same message more than once. How do you make processing safe?

rubric.1: Knows duplicates happen but has no concrete handling.
rubric.2: Makes the consumer idempotent using a deduplication key or idempotent write.
rubric.3: Explains the delivery guarantee, a concrete dedup design and how it was tested.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: A downstream API times out. Should your integration retry, and how?
expected_topics: timeouts do not mean no side effect

rubric.0: Retries indefinitely or never considers side effects.
rubric.1: Retries with a fixed delay without considering duplicates.
rubric.2: Retries idempotent operations with backoff and a limit.
rubric.3: Explains side-effect risk, idempotency keys, backoff with jitter and overload protection.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: What is a dead-letter queue and how do you operate one?

rubric.0: Does not know what a dead-letter queue is.
rubric.1: Knows the definition but not how to operate it.
rubric.2: Explains thresholds, monitoring and investigating failed messages.
rubric.3: Describes an operational process including alerting, root-cause analysis and safe redrive.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: How would you design an API so a client can safely retry a payment or order creation request?

rubric.0: No mechanism; relies on the client not retrying.
rubric.1: Suggests checking for duplicates without a clear key strategy.
rubric.2: Uses a client-generated idempotency key and returns the stored result on retry.
rubric.3: Full design including key scope, expiry, concurrent duplicates and mismatched payloads.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: A request fails somewhere across three services. How do you find where it failed?

rubric.1: Checks logs in each service manually without correlation.
rubric.2: Uses correlation or trace IDs across services to follow the request.
rubric.3: Describes tracing propagation, structured logs and a real investigation including root cause and fix validation.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: A partner API starts returning 503 errors intermittently. How do you investigate and protect your integration?

rubric.1: Recognises a server-side problem but has no plan.
rubric.2: Interprets 503 correctly, applies backoff and monitors the impact.
rubric.3: Structured investigation, protective measures (backoff, circuit breaking, queuing) and partner escalation.

records.title: Integration Engineer question bank
records.question: What do you log in an integration to make troubleshooting possible, and what must never be logged?
expected_topics: exclude tokens, secrets and personal data

rubric.0: Logs everything including secrets, or logs nothing useful.
rubric.1: Logs some context but is unclear about sensitive data.
rubric.2: Logs consistent context with correlation IDs and excludes secrets and personal data.
rubric.3: Explains a logging standard, redaction approach and how logs were used in a real incident.
